All Triangles Are Isosceles?

ParadoxesLogicInvariants
Game: Find the mistake in a proof that every triangle is isosceles.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B and C, then tick "Honest drawing" to see where the picture was cheating.
Look for the math

The argument looks solid: build P from the angle bisector and perpendicular bisector, drop two perpendiculars, match three pairs of congruent triangles, and conclude that two sides are equal. Yet all triangles are not isosceles. Where does it break?

The chain of congruences

Triangles AMP and BMP are congruent by SAS, so AP = BP. Right triangles CPU and CPV are congruent by ASA, so CU = CV and PU = PV. Then right triangles APU and BPV are congruent by SSS, giving AU = BV. Adding, the proof claims AC = AU + CU = BV + CV = BC. Every congruence is correct — the addition is not.

Where the picture lies

The angle bisector from C and the perpendicular bisector of AB always meet on the circumcircle of ABC: the bisector cuts arc AB in half, and so does the perpendicular bisector through the circumcenter. When P is on the circle, one of the feet U, V lies outside its side, so one of the two "additions" is really a subtraction. The applet's original diagram quietly shifts P inside to hide this.

What the check found

The logic test builds hundreds of random acute, scalene triangles. In the honest construction P lies on the circumcircle in every case, exactly one foot falls outside its side, and the three congruent pairs really are equal while the two sides are not. The misleading construction always puts both feet on the segments, which is why the fake proof looks convincing. Try dragging C until the triangle is nearly isosceles — the trick becomes harder to see.

Tick "More info" and switch between the two drawings. Which of the two additions, AC = AU + CU or BC = BV + CV, is wrong in your triangle?
